text:
Chris Dixon on the "second-order effects" behind a16z's early bets on Oculus, drones, and crypto:

"I joined the firm in 2013. I talked to Marc and Ben, and I said, 'Hey, I wanna do this crazy stuff,' and they were like, 'Great.'"

"That led to a couple of themes at the time, and they're all kind of what I would call kinda second-order effects. You had smartphones obviously start in 2007, and by 2013 had gotten mainstream, and there were all these kind of first-order effects like building apps on top."

"But a second-order effect was that you had the components of smartphones. You had sensors and chips getting better and better, and maybe people could repurpose those in different ways."

"We invested in Oculus as an example, and that was really kind of a reconfigured smartphone. Skydio, that was one of our investments from back then that was, at the beginning, kind of a reconfigured smartphone."

"Crypto, I think at the time was kind of a downstream effect to me of sort of the open-source software movement morphing into services and also kind of a result of social media where you could have these communities form without mainstream acceptance and coalesce around these blockchains."

@cdixon

Chris Dixon on a16z Frontier's investing philosophy, and why being too early is better than being too late:

"We believe that basically every good idea that we've ever seen that involved technology has eventually worked or we believe will work, if it hasn't worked yet."

"Almost everything that ended up working had a precursor that didn't work and maybe was 10 years too early. And that's the hardest thing in technology is to predict the timing of these things."

"There's the technology, there's the culture, there's the business environment, there's the political environment. There's so many factors that go into these things and having it all line up."

"Specifically in the Frontier Fund, we want to err on the side of being too early."

@cdixon

Chris Dixon on the deal that built the internet, why AI is breaking it, and the "great reconfiguration" that comes next:

"I call it the internet's covenant, which is sort of a deal between the distribution side of the internet, Google, Facebook, and so forth, and the content side, news sites, travel sites, whatever it might be."

"The websites that make money on ads and conversions and other things can no longer do that. You see the early signs of this, like Stack Overflow and some other websites where the traffic dropped precipitously when you had sort of AI replacements."

"Many of these transactions will still happen. They just won't happen in the way they were happening... There's a bunch of businesses that are built on the human attention economy that will have challenges."

"On the entrepreneur side, there's a chance to rethink these things from first principles and say, 'Okay, what does a better internet look like?'"

"I think this is gonna happen over the next, let's call it decade, you're gonna have this kinda great reconfiguration of the internet and how the economics work, how the attention flows, how knowledge is shared, how people produce things together, collaborate."

@cdixon

text:
AI can now find vulnerabilities with internet-scale impact. Greg Brockman on why defenders can hold the advantage, what OpenAI did to secure itself, and its $1B commitment to secure critical infrastructure:

"This [cyber] capability broadly diffused, I think is something that will really empower threat actors in new ways. And I think that defenders need to use this time before that technology's broadly available to secure themselves."

"At OpenAI, we took 25% of our production engineers and said, 'Sorry, all your projects are on hold. You are now defending... You're going to use the models to find all the holes.' And we found a number of serious issues and we fixed them."

"You want to be in this tight loop of new cyber capability drops, you deploy it against your systems, you find the new holes, and ideally, you've managed to automate this... If you can do that at machine speed, I think the defenders will be advantaged in deeply significant ways."

"Not every organization will have the capital required to do it. So we have a billion-dollar commitment to frontline defenders, so to organizations that we all rely on every day in our communities, to access our models to secure themselves."

"I've never met a CISO who felt that they were appropriately resourced... Now is a moment where we actually have a real both motivation to do it and a real ability to do it."

@gdb
